author: ohtadmin
title: BLIZZARD BLASTS ISLAND
text:
The 2,000-mile-long blizzard that swept across the nation reached the island Sunday and dropped about a foot of snow before departing Jamestown.
Nobody lost power, however, and roads were passable by Monday morning due to the community “respecting and complying” with the parking ban, said Jamie Campbell, chief of police.
“We were also fortunate that motorists largely stayed off the roads,” he added.
Campbell said there were only two vehicles that were parked on the road. Both owners were contacted, however, and the cars were moved without police having to issue tickets.
Campbell credited Sgt. Jason Hopkins and patrolman Liam Robberson for shoveling a car free on Route 138 after the driver, “an essential worker,” got stuck in the snow near the East Shore Road exit.
Police also responded to a home after a woman complained of having no heat.
“We were able to help with a temporary fix so she could remain safely in her home,” Campbell said. “The shelter was prepared to open if needed, but fortunately, it was not necessary.”
Aside from those incidents, “there were no accidents or major issues during the storm, and no serious calls for service,” he added.
The chief of the fire department, Howie Tighe, said it responded to “a few medical calls” and an alarm at the library during the storm. The department, regardless, was prepared for a busier evening with crews, both firefighters and emergency medical technicians, staying overnight at the firehouse for the duration of the storm.
Tighe is asking homeowners to “remove snow the best you can if you have a hydrant near your property lines.” He also is reminding them to make sure their exterior vents on the sides of their homes are clear.
“This time of year,” he said, “we see an increase in carbon monoxide calls related to blocked vents.”
McQuade’s closed early at 1 p.m. Sunday without selling out of bread, milk and eggs, which are the staples for families expecting to be snowed in. Cumberland Farms ran out of gas before the storm and did not refill until Tuesday night.
Steve Sherman, owner of Jamestown Hardware, said they sold out of shovels, gas cans and ice melt, which has been a challenge to resupply. He closed his store around 11 a.m. Sunday but said residents were proactive and bought their supplies ahead of time.
“We were busy for days before the storm,” he said.
Town Administrator Ed Mello said 14 pieces of equipment were deployed to remove the snow, which at times fell at 2 inches hourly. Overtime due to the storm is estimated to cost $11,400. The cost of materials and fuel, however, has not been determined.
The schools, senior center, transfer station, library, recreation center and Town Hall were closed Monday due to “adverse weather and road conditions.

The department, regardless, was prepared for a busier evening with crews, both firefighters and emergency medical technicians, staying overnight at the firehouse for the duration of the storm.
